title: Archery in the dark
hookLine: a lamp blows out at dinner, a boy's hand still finds his mouth, and Arjuna learns what practice is
carry: abhyasa: practice, repeated, steadies the mind
last: PANCHANG: THE HOLY DAYS COME ROUND.

lines: HOW DOES ANYONE KEEP IT UP?
A BOY, A BOW, A LAMP BLOWN OUT.
cards: Sixty days ago this camp began with the breath you already have. Since then: a mantra, a shelf with a lamp and a flower, a flame at sunset, a way into the temple, a year of festivals. Lovely pieces.
But how does anyone keep them going, on a tired Tuesday, for years? The old stories answer with a boy, a bow, and a lamp that blew out.

teach.b: When the Pandava princes were boys, they learned archery from their teacher, Drona. One night, the story goes, Arjuna was eating dinner when a gust of wind blew out the lamp.

teach.h: HIS HAND STILL FINDS THE WAY.
teach.b: In the pitch dark he kept eating, and noticed something: his hand still found his mouth, every time, without looking. It knew the way because it had done it so often. So that's what practice does, he thought.
He took his bow out into the night and began to shoot in the dark. Drona heard the bowstring, came out, held him, and promised to make him an archer without equal.

teach.h: THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.
teach.b: Years later, the same Arjuna tells Krishna, in the Gita, that the mind is restless, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna doesn't argue.
He says the mind is held by two things: abhyasa, practice, repeated, and vairagya, letting go. That's why Hindu practice is daily. A lamp lit every morning.
A name said on a mala, around and around. Arti at sunset, the same song. It isn't that once doesn't count.
It's that repetition trains the mind the way the dark trained Arjuna's hand, until the practice holds you on the days you can't hold it.

So camp three closes by setting your table: one thing for the morning, a breath, a mantra or a lamp; one for sunset, a flame or just facing the light; one for the week, a temple visit or a small fast; and your festivals for the year.

teach.h: SMALL ENOUGH TO DO IN THE DARK.
teach.b: Small enough to do in the dark. Tomorrow, camp four: the Gita, in order.

how: Many Hindus keep a small daily round, a morning lamp or prayer, japa on a mala, an evening arti, and add weekly observances and the family's festivals; the Gita (6.35) names abhyasa, repeated practice, with letting go, as what steadies the restless mind.

practice: Choose your four pieces. For the morning, one thing you could do tomorrow before your phone: a slow breath, one round of your mantra, or one lamp. For sunset, a flame, or just turning toward the light.

For the week, a temple visit, a small fast, or sun salutations on Sunday. For the year, your festivals. Now picture doing the morning one half asleep, without thinking, the way Arjuna's hand found its way in the dark.
That's where abhyasa is taking you.

wordCard.voice: Abhyasa. Practice, repeated: Krishna's word in the Gita for how the restless mind is held. Said to the same Arjuna who once practiced in the dark.

orig.note: Sanskrit: practice, repeated. the word Krishna uses in the Gita for steadying the mind.
